tone_statements.citation: Singler, John Victor (1985). The status of lexical associations and the obligatory contour principle in the analysis of tone languages. In African Linguistics. Essays in Memory of M.W.K. Semikenke. John Benjamins Publishing Company. 491ff pp.
tone_statements.quote: A different type of violation of the OCP exists in Klao, a Kru language spoken in Liberia. Here the contrast is between di- and tri-syllabic forms having, for example, the tone melody M H, as illustrated by [nane] 'to speak' and [popolo] 'wind, breeze'. [...] Lightfoot (1974) posits three underlying level tones, L, M, and H, and no contours. Singler (1979) presents several pieces of evidence in favor of Lightfoot's analysis (and against Elimelech's). The present discussion assumes the analysis put forth by Lightfoot.
tone_statements.locator: printed p. 494; footnote 4 printed p. 505; footnote 5 (Low-Tone Raising after long vowels)
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: First-hand in part (Singler 1979 ms 'Tone in Klao'); three level tones L, M, H, no underlying contours; mapping runs left to right; Low-Tone Raising rule after a long vowel (fn 5). Not graded against a catalog entry here (packet carries only the Mende entry).

Cahiers Ivoiriens de Recherche Linguistique 6: 9-33 (Communications presentees au 1er colloque international sur les langues kru); and Lightfoot, Nancy. 1980. tone_statements.quote: p. 9, fn. 1: "Klao is the language which is referred to in older linguistic literature and by speakers of English in Liberia as Kru. The data in this paper are from Talo Klao, the dialect spoken in Nifu, Sasstown Territory, Liberia. My consultants were Samson Tiklo and Dubel Nyakun, to whom I am profoundly indebted. The system used for marking tone in this paper is the following: V́ High Tone V̄ Mid Tone V̀ Low Tone" || pp. 10-11: "The behavior of these suffixes with regard to tone requires further investigation and will not be discussed here except to note that, as a general statement regarding these suffixes, those which are identical segmentally tend to have identical tonal behavior as well. Thus, tone does not--for the most part--serve to distinguish and disambiguate these suffixes from one another." || p. 20: "As in the case of verb-attaching suffixes, a description of the behavior of these suffixes with regard to tone has been deferred until further investigation has been completed."

tone_statements.summary: No catalog entry. The article is a morphosyntactic description of verb suffixes, not a prosodic description. tone_statements.citation: Elimelech, Baruch. 1974. On the reality of underlying contour tones. In Ian Maddieson (ed.), The Tone Tome: Studies on Tone from the UCLA Tone Project (UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 27), 74-83.
tone_statements.quote: A situation which is similar to the hypothetical language in (9) exists in Kru*. In this language there is a High, a Low, a Rising and a Falling tone. ... Downdrift also exists in Kru. What is of interest here is that the rising tone in citation forms is realized as a rise from a High to a Superhigh pitch [p. 78] ... There are four contrasting tones on monosyllabic words, exemplified in (17) [p. 79] ... Since there are only four possible tone patterns on bisyllabic words, corresponding exactly to the four tone patterns on monosyllabic words, we can assume that tone is a feature assigned to words (or morphemes) in this language and not to segments or syllables. [p. 80] ... Thus, we may conclude that tone is a property of words in Kru and must therefore be represented by a suprasegmental matrix. [p. 81]
tone_statements.locator: printed pp. 78-82; footnote p. 78 names the dialect and informant; examples (11)-(24)
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: First-hand: 'This study is based solely on the speech of Mr. Sayon Jackson who served as the informant' (footnote, p. 78). Four word tones H, L, R, F on monosyllables; bisyllabic patterns L-L, H-H, H-R, H-F only (19), so tone is a word-level (suprasegmental) property mapped onto syllables. Rising tone starts at the end-point of the preceding tone and rises to Superhigh; a simplification rule R ->

sources.note: Nothing on stress.
